title: Chapter 30
paragraphs: The raging tempest rushed whistling between the wheels of the carriages, around the scaffolding, and round the corner of the station. The carriages, posts, people, everything in sight was covered with snow on one side, and was being thickly covered with more. For a moment there would come a lull in the storm, but then it would swoop down again with such force it seemed impossible to stand against it. Meanwhile men ran back and forth, talking merrily, their steps crackling on the platform as they kept opening and closing the big doors. The bent shadow of a man glided by at her feet, and she heard the sound of a hammer on iron. "Hand over that telegram!" came an angry voice out of the stormy darkness on the other side. "This way! No. 28!" several different voices shouted again, and muffled figures ran by, covered with snow. Two gentlemen with lit cigarettes passed her. She drew another deep breath of the fresh air, and had just taken her hand out of her muff to grab the doorpost and get back into the carriage when another man in a military overcoat, very close beside her, stepped between her and the flickering light of the lamppost. She looked round, and that instant recognized Vronsky's face. Putting his hand to the peak of his cap, he bowed to her and asked whether there was anything she wanted, whether he could be of any service. For a fairly long while she gazed at him without answering, and, in spite of the shadow he was standing in, she saw, or fancied she saw, both the expression of his face and his eyes. It was again that look of reverent ecstasy that had so worked on her the day before. More than once in the past few days, and again only a few moments before, she had told herself that Vronsky was for her only one of the hundreds of young men, forever exactly the same, that one meets everywhere, and that she would never allow herself to give him a thought. But now at the first instant of meeting him, she was seized by a feeling of joyful pride. She had no need to ask why he had come. She knew as certainly as if he had told her that he was here in order to be where she was.
"I didn't realize you were traveling. What have you come for?" she said, letting fall the hand with which she had gripped the doorpost. Irrepressible delight and eagerness lit her face.
"What have I come for?" he repeated, looking straight into her eyes. "You know — I have come to be where you are," he said. "I can't help it."

At that moment the wind, as if overcoming all obstacles, sent the snow flying from the carriage roofs, and clanked some sheet of iron it had torn loose, while the hoarse whistle of the engine roared in front, mournful and gloomy. The whole awfulness of the storm seemed even more splendid to her now. He had said what her soul longed to hear, though she feared it with her reason. She made no answer, and in her face he saw a conflict.
"Forgive me, if you dislike what I said," he said humbly.
He had spoken courteously, deferentially, yet so firmly, so stubbornly, that for a long while she could make no answer.
"What you say is wrong, and I beg you, if you're a good man, to forget what you've said, as I forget it," she said at last.
"Not one word, not one gesture of yours shall I, could I, ever forget..."

"Enough, enough!" she cried, trying hard to give a stern expression to her face, into which he was gazing greedily. And, clutching at the cold doorpost, she clambered up the steps and got rapidly into the corridor of the carriage. But in the little corridor she paused, going over in her mind what had happened. Though she could not recall her own words or his, she sensed instinctively that the moment's conversation had brought them frighteningly closer; and she was panic-stricken and blissful at it. After standing still for a few seconds, she went into the carriage and sat down in her place. The overstrained condition that had tormented her before not only came back but intensified, reaching such a pitch that she was afraid every minute that something would snap inside her from the excessive tension. She did not sleep all night. But in that nervous tension, and in the visions filling her imagination, there was nothing disagreeable or gloomy: on the contrary there was something blissful, glowing, and exhilarating. Toward morning Anna sank into a doze, sitting in her place, and when she woke it was daylight and the train was nearing Petersburg. At once thoughts of home, of husband and son, and the details of that day and the next came over her.

At Petersburg, as soon as the train stopped and she got out, the first person who caught her attention was her husband. "Oh, mercy! why do his ears look like that?" she thought, looking at his frigid and imposing figure, and especially the ears that struck her in that moment as propping up the brim of his round hat. Catching sight of her, he came toward her, his lips falling into their habitual sarcastic smile, his big, tired eyes looking straight at her. An unpleasant sensation gripped at her heart when she met his obstinate and weary glance, as though she had expected to find him different. She was especially struck by the feeling of dissatisfaction with herself that she felt on meeting him. That feeling was an intimate, familiar one, like the consciousness of hypocrisy that she felt in her relations with her husband. But until now she had not noticed the feeling; now she was clearly and painfully aware of it.

"Yes — as you can see, your tender spouse, as devoted as in the first year of our marriage, burned with impatience to see you," he said in his deliberate, high-pitched voice, in the tone he almost always took with her — a tone that mocked anyone who might say in earnest what he was saying.
"And is this all the reward," he said, "for my ardor? He's quite well..."
